Probability of success
rows.explainer:
This accounts for our internal estimate of how likely a non-profit is to be successful in implementation. i.e., succesfully delivering the program, not the effects of the program itself. Failure modes include not being able to partner with health facilities, for instance. 

When this is used to calculate potential disbenefits we take the most sceptical view imaginable: We imagine a world where somehow the charity manages to have costs on the population but zero benefits, like the beneficiaries receive the SMSes and get bus tickets to the hospital but there are no vaccine available when they get there. This is a very negative assumption. But I can see a case for making negative assumptions and it also has very minimal effect on the actual output.

source.quote: a 12% observed reduction in the risk of all-cause mortality ... (risk ratio (RR) 0.88, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.83 to 0.93 ...); a random-effects meta-analysis showed ... (24% reduction: RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.88)

rows.explainer: Changed for consistency. Ambitious Impact's sheet enters 0.76, the risk ratio of child death with vitamin A supplements (a random-effects estimate), but its formulas use this cell as an efficacy, the share of deaths prevented (Main CEA!C82 × mortality × 70% addressable). A risk ratio of 0.76 means 24% of deaths are prevented, not 76%. Its cited source, the Cochrane review (Imdad et al. 2017), gives a 12% reduction as its main, high-quality estimate (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.83–0.93), and 24% under a random-effects model. We use 0.12, with 0.07 (the top of the fixed-effect interval) to 0.24 (the random-effects estimate) as the range; the evaluator view keeps AIM's 0.76.

summary: Ambitious Impact's 2023 estimate for a new charity sending SMS and voice reminders to caregivers so more children complete their vaccinations, modelled for Angola. The idea Notify Health was founded to run. A re-implementation of AIM's spreadsheet, traced from its cost per DALY counting the charity's costs and the health system's and families' costs ($78; $39 counting the charity's costs alone; its Nigeria tab gives $81). In our view the vitamin A benefit uses the Cochrane review's 12% cut in child deaths, not AIM's 76%.
